article_title: Patterns of action transitions in online collaborative problem solving: A network analysis approach
citation: Shupin Li · Johanna Pöysä-Tarhonen · Päivi Häkkinen (2022). Patterns of action transitions in online collaborative problem solving: A network analysis approach. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2022) 17:191–223 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09369-7
title: Transition networks of action sequences analyzed with five SNA measures (nodes, density, degree centralization, reciprocity, triad census) for dyadic CPS process data
description: A methodological artifact integrating social network analysis with CPS assessment: for each dyad, actions (e.g., drag to move an object, type in a chat window) are nodes and directed weighted links represent transitions where "the first action is followed by the second action in sequence". In the Olive Oil task, analysis relied on "14,448 log file events conducted by 83 pairs". Five measures capture transition patterns: numbers of existing nodes (actions conducted), weighted density (average frequency of transitions among actions), Freeman degree centralization (dispersion of attempts given to different actions), reciprocity (extent to which pairs revisit the previous action immediately), and numbers of the 16 triadic patterns. Self-loops were excluded, and isolated nodes were added so networks had identical node sets for comparison.
requirements: Sequential process data with order-relevant action timestamps from a computer-based CPS environment, with actions categorized (system, transfer, other operational, chat actions) so transitions between different actions can be modeled as weighted directed links.
constraints: The contents of students' chat messages were excluded from the analysis; self-loops (repeating the same action) were excluded because interest was in transitions between different actions; analysis used the Olive Oil task only.
target_learners: paired students in computer-based problem solving assessment
target_learning_goals: analyzing collaborative problem solving processes and productivity via action transition patterns
examples: Fig. 2 visualizes the combined transition network of all 83 pairs, with node size by indegree, edge sizes as weights divided by 150, and colors distinguishing transitions inside, outside, and across the most efficient path.
key_sources: Shupin Li · Johanna Pöysä-Tarhonen · Päivi Häkkinen (2022). Patterns of action transitions in online collaborative problem solving: A network analysis approach. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn (2022) 17:191–223 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-022-09369-7

article_title: Social Network Analysis in E-Learning Environments: A Preliminary Systematic Review
citation: Cela, K.L., Sicilia, M.Á. & Sánchez, S. (2015). Social Network Analysis in E-Learning Environments: A Preliminary Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9276-0
title: Social network analysis as an approach to understanding and improving e-learning systems
description: The review frames social network analysis (SNA) as a methodological approach for describing and analysing network behaviours in e-learning. It notes SNA "has proven extremely powerful at describing and analysing network behaviours in business, economics and medicine, but its application to e-learning has been relatively limited." The review positions SNA as a way to understand and improve e-learning systems, operationalised through measures such as centrality and density applied to learner interaction networks, most often in forum-based one-mode networks.
requirements: Interaction data from an e-learning environment (e.g. forum posts) that can be represented as a network of relations between members.
constraints: Application to e-learning has been relatively limited compared with business, economics and medicine, per the review.
target_learning_goals: Understanding and improving interaction patterns and course design in e-learning systems
examples: The review's included studies applied SNA methods to analyse interaction patterns in discussion forums in e-learning courses.
key_sources: Cela, K.L., Sicilia, M.Á. & Sánchez, S. (2015). Social Network Analysis in E-Learning Environments: A Preliminary Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-014-9276-0

article_title: Reassessing Aptitude: Introduction to a Special Issue in Honor of Richard E. Snow
citation: Patrick C. Kyllonen & Susanne P. Lajoie (2003). Reassessing Aptitude: Introduction to a Special Issue in Honor of Richard E. Snow. Educational Psychologist, 38(2), 79–83. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3802_2
title: Snow's transactional conception of aptitude: aptitude as person–situation transactions rather than a static trait
description: The article presents Snow's conceptualization of aptitude, developed in Corno et al. (2002), as emphasizing transactions between personal characteristics and the affordances of particular situations. As summarized from Lohman, persons bring propensities and situations make some actions more likely, and "which propensities function as aptitudes (or inaptitudes) depend ultimately on the transactions that occur on a moment by moment basis". This reframes aptitude as dynamic rather than a fixed test score.
requirements: Requires treating aptitude as any personal characteristic that affects learning, including cognitive, affective, and conative characteristics
constraints: The article notes Snow's own research on will, determination, cognitive flexibility, fluidity, and playfulness remained speculative and was not tested empirically
target_learning_goals: understanding how learner characteristics relate to learning outcomes
examples: The Stanford Aptitude Seminar completed the posthumous project as the book Remaking the Concept of Aptitude: Extending the Legacy of Richard E. Snow (Corno et al., 2002)
key_sources: Patrick C. Kyllonen & Susanne P. Lajoie (2003). Reassessing Aptitude: Introduction to a Special Issue in Honor of Richard E. Snow. Educational Psychologist, 38(2), 79–83. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3802_2

article_title: A systematic review of AI literacy scales
citation: Tomáš Lintner. (2024). A systematic review of AI literacy scales. npj Science of Learning 9:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00264-4
title: SNAIL: a general-population self-report scale with the three-factor TUCAPA model of AI literacy
description: SNAIL (Scale for the Assessment of Non-experts' AI Literacy) is a 31-item general-population scale developed from a Delphi expert study, whose exploratory factor analysis yielded the three-factor TUCAPA model: "technical understanding, critical appraisal, and practical application". It has been revalidated in Turkish and in German for learning-gains use. The review rates it a promising instrument with high evidence for structural validity and internal consistency, but notes an indicated floor effect, with almost half of items having >15% lowest-score responses.
requirements: Content validity on the general population still needs to be checked, and the floor effect investigated, per the review
constraints: Only limited evidence for reliability and responsiveness due to a small longitudinal sample size
examples: Most participants complete the scale within 10 minutes, making it feasible for quick assessment
key_sources: Tomáš Lintner. (2024). A systematic review of AI literacy scales. npj Science of Learning 9:50. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00264-4

article_title: Developing educational materials about risks on social network sites: a design based research approach
citation: Vanderhoven, E., Schellens, T., Vanderlinde, R., & Valcke, M. (2015). Developing educational materials about risks on social network sites: A design-based research approach. Ghent University. https://biblio.ugent.be
title: Four context-sensitive design principles for educational materials about SNS risks
description: Through reflection on all eight studies, the authors revised their initial design principles into four contextually sensitive principles: individual reflection is critical; simulated environments are sufficient; involving parents is beneficial; and a short-term intervention is sufficient. Table 5 maps each revised principle to the initial principle it reinterprets, e.g. collaborative learning becomes "Individual reflection is critical" and authentic setting becomes "Simulated environments are sufficient".
requirements: Materials should build in time for individual reflection before peer discussion
A homework task completed in collaboration with parents is proposed to involve all parents
constraints: The authors acknowledge the principles are context-specific, which jeopardizes external validity; generalizability to other behaviors and cultures requires future research
target_learning_goals: awareness of contact risks on SNSs
safer attitudes and behavior regarding privacy and cyberbullying
examples: The final package combined a one-hour course with a homework task done together with parents, which appeared sufficient to obtain the proposed goals
key_sources: Vanderhoven, E., Schellens, T., Vanderlinde, R., & Valcke, M. (2015). Developing educational materials about risks on social network sites: A design-based research approach. Ghent University. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-015-9415-4

article_title: Developing educational materials about risks on social network sites: a design based research approach
citation: Vanderhoven, E., Schellens, T., Vanderlinde, R., & Valcke, M. (2015). Developing educational materials about risks on social network sites: A design-based research approach. Ghent University. https://biblio.ugent.be
title: One-hour SNS contact-risks educational package with syllabus, teacher manual, and parental homework task
description: The developed intervention is a package for secondary education focusing on contact risks (privacy risks, cyberbullying, sexual solicitation), consisting of a pupil syllabus and a teacher manual, with every course lasting one hour. Its fixed structure includes an introduction, an individual exercise on a simulated worst-case SNS profile, class discussion, a voting-cards game, and theory with real-life examples, applying the prevention and constructivist principles in Table 3.
requirements: A teacher manual with learning goals
Materials kept clear, concise and not time-consuming, as stakeholders requested
constraints: The simulated worst-case profile contained so many risks that pupils found it less realistic and could dissociate from it
target_learning_goals: heightened awareness of contact risks on SNSs
decreased unsafe attitudes and behavior on SNSs
examples: Pupils answered questions about a simulated worst-case scenario SNS profile, discussed answers in class, and responded to statements with green or red voting cards
key_sources: Vanderhoven, E., Schellens, T., Vanderlinde, R., & Valcke, M. (2015). Developing educational materials about risks on social network sites: A design-based research approach. Ghent University. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-015-9415-4

article_title: The Effect of Using Self-Monitoring Strategies in Social Studies Course on Self-Monitoring, Self-Regulation and Academic Achievement
citation: Arslantas, S. & Kurnaz, A. (2017). The effect of using self -monitoring strategies in social studies course on self -monitoring, self -regulation and academic achievement. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 3(2), 452-463. https://doi.org/10.21890/ijres.327905
title: Snyder's Self-Monitoring Theory: individual differences in controlling self-presentation, with behavioral and academic self-monitoring as two components
description: The article frames its intervention with Snyder's (1974) Self-Monitoring Theory, according to which "individuals differ in the extent to which they control their self -presentation in social interactions". High self-monitors closely monitor themselves, follow social cues and care about social expectations, while low self-monitors act from internal tendencies and show steady behaviors. The theory distinguishes behavioral self-monitoring, described as more comprehensive, from academic self-monitoring, which underpins metacognitive strategy use and learning-to-learn. Self-monitoring itself has two dimensions: self-observation (examining one's own processes, feelings and behaviors) and self-control (keeping monitored behaviors in mind so intended behaviors are repeated).
requirements: The article states an ideal, balanced level of self-monitoring is desired: individuals should monitor themselves to a certain extent, since levels that are too high or too low indicate problems in learning and behavior processes
constraints: The article notes high self-monitoring can cause individuals to compromise themselves for others and feel incompetent, while low self-monitoring can create a misleading sense of perfection
examples: The study operationalized the theory through strategies such as control lists, rubrics, self-created graphics, and self-evaluation in a Social Studies course
key_sources: Arslantas, S. & Kurnaz, A. (2017). The effect of using self -monitoring strategies in social studies course on self -monitoring, self -regulation and academic achievement. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 3(2), 452-463. https://doi.org/10.21890/ijres.327905

article_title: The Curious Case of Centrality Measures: A Large-Scale Empirical Investigation
citation: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas. (2022). The Curious Case of Centrality Measures: A Large-Scale Empirical Investigation. Journal of Learning Analytics. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2022.7415
title: Social Network Analysis centrality measures as a framework for quantifying collaborative learning interactions
description: The article describes SNA as offering "methods for the study of social networks in the form of visualization and mathematical analysis." Centrality measures provide "a quantification of node connectedness, interactions, position, or importance in the network." Six centrality measures within three categories (degree, short-path, and eigenvector-based) have been used in CSCL as indicators of student success, each operationalizing a distinct aspect of participation and social positioning.
requirements: Network data constructed from post-reply interactions among learners in collaborative settings
constraints: The literature cites more than two hundred centrality measures, but very few are used in education
target_learners: higher education students in problem-based learning courses
target_learning_goals: quantifying participation and social positioning in collaborative learning
examples: The study operationalized out-degree as effort and participation, in-degree as worthiness of contributions, and eigenvector centrality as student positioning and strength of relationships.
key_sources: Mohammed Saqr, Sonsoles López-Pernas. (2022). The Curious Case of Centrality Measures: A Large-Scale Empirical Investigation. Journal of Learning Analytics. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2022.7415

article_title: Impact of SNAPPS-based teaching on diagnostic accuracy and academic achievement in pathology residents.
citation: Khanke Shraddha; Buch Pankti; Buch Archana; Gore Charusheela. (2026). Impact of SNAPPS-based teaching on diagnostic accuracy and academic achievement in pathology residents. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09668-9
title: SNAPPS: a six-step learner-centred case-presentation model (Summarise, Narrow, Analyse, Probe, Plan, Self-directed learning)
description: SNAPPS is a learner-centred teaching model whose acronym stands for "Summarise, Narrow, Analyse, Probe, Plan, and Self-directed learning". Originally developed for outpatient teaching, it structures case presentations so residents summarise findings, narrow differentials, analyse them, probe the preceptor, plan management or investigations, and pursue self-directed learning. This study adapted it to pathology case write-ups and presentations, assessing each component on a 5-point checklist.
requirements: Trained preceptors calibrated on the SNAPPS checklist to score consistently
Cases with gross specimens and microscopic slides suitable for differential-diagnosis reasoning
constraints: The article notes its application in pathology residency had previously been underexplored
Self-directed learning proved the hardest component, limited by resident time
examples: Residents presented the same cases under SNAPPS headings after one week of preparation, evaluated with the six-component checklist
key_sources: Khanke Shraddha; Buch Pankti; Buch Archana; Gore Charusheela. (2026). Impact of SNAPPS-based teaching on diagnostic accuracy and academic achievement in pathology residents. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09668-9

article_title: Social network analysis as a technology-enhanced assessment tool for collaborative skills in medical PBL.
citation: Ahmad Azman Ahmad Hathim, Tiong Nee, Kamarudin Mohammad Arif, Zamzuri Zamira Hasanah. (2026). Social network analysis as a technology-enhanced assessment tool for collaborative skills in medical PBL. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09397-z
title: SNA-based technology-enhanced assessment framework for collaborative competence in PBL
description: The article operationalises social network analysis as an assessment output for PBL: directed, weighted group networks are built by combining a validated five-item collaboration rubric with ranked top-three peer nominations into hybrid edge weights (a 50:50 mixture). Centrality measures act as "assessment outputs, providing each student with quantifiable indicators of their collaborative engagement and social positioning within the group", mapped to CBME competency domains such as peer-recognised collaborative reliability and brokerage.
requirements: Complete relational data: valid network-level analyses require all members of a PBL group to respond, so recruitment is at group level.
A validated peer collaboration scale and a peer nomination instrument administered via authenticated accounts with self-nominations disabled.
constraints: Out-degree was excluded because the fixed top-three nomination cap restricts its variability and interpretive value.
The article calls the CGPA alignment preliminary validity evidence and notes further longitudinal and multilevel research is warranted.
target_learners: Year 1 and Year 2 undergraduate medical students in PBL groups
target_learning_goals: Collaborative communication and teamwork competence in problem-based learning
examples: Applied to 17 complete PBL groups (72 Year 1, 94 Year 2 students), capturing 482 interactions as directed, weighted networks.
key_sources: Ahmad Azman Ahmad Hathim, Tiong Nee, Kamarudin Mohammad Arif, Zamzuri Zamira Hasanah. (2026). Social network analysis as a technology-enhanced assessment tool for collaborative skills in medical PBL. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09397-z

article_title: Guiding Midwives to Precept Students: Two Evidence-Based Models.
citation: Taylor Margaret C., Diaz Hannah L. (2026). Guiding Midwives to Precept Students: Two Evidence‐Based Models. Journal of Midwifery & Women's Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/jmwh.70075
title: SNAPPS: a learner-driven six-step case presentation model
description: SNAPPS (Summarize, Narrow, Analyze, Probe, Plan, Select), developed by Wolpaw and colleagues in 2003, is a learner-driven model with six steps: summarize the history and findings; narrow the differential to 2 or 3 possibilities; analyze by comparing and contrasting; probe the preceptor about uncertainties; plan management; and select a case-related issue for self-directed learning. It was developed to move students away from the teacher-controlled process, so students "take ownership of the diagnostic and management process" and are not penalized for incorrect diagnoses or asking questions. The article proposes it for advanced midwifery learners.
requirements: The student be prepared and engaged in the clinical reasoning process
A preceptor willing to serve as a knowledge resource when probed
constraints: Better suited for more advanced learners because of their greater knowledge base, though the article reports that with support and practice even new learners can benefit
Originally developed for the outpatient medical setting
target_learners: Advanced midwifery students on clinical rotations
examples: The article describes students probing the preceptor about uncertainties, revealing knowledge deficits while the preceptor corrects missteps in clinical thinking
key_sources: Taylor Margaret C., Diaz Hannah L. (2026). Guiding Midwives to Precept Students: Two Evidence‐Based Models. Journal of Midwifery & Women's Health. https://doi.org/10.1111/jmwh.70075

article_title: The effect of strengthening nurse practitioners' competency in occupational health services for agricultural workers exposed to pesticides in primary care units, Thailand: a before-and-after study.
citation: Napamon P, Jirapongsuwan A, Kalampakorn S, Siri S. (2025). The effect of strengthening nurse practitioners’ competency in occupational health services for agricultural workers exposed to pesticides in primary care units, Thailand: a before-and-after study. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2025.22.14
title: SNPCOHS program: a 4-week, 10-hour e-learning intervention with 10 modules for NPs in primary care units
description: The Strengthening Nurse Practitioners’ Competency in Occupational Health Service program is a 4-week, 10-hour blended e-learning intervention comprising "10 modules covering key topics such as pesticide fundamentals, occupational health laws, screening and referral, primary care, risk communication, and the role of nurses in occupational health services." Activities include self-paced e-learning with video clips, post-lesson quizzes, case-based assignments, and online discussions with peer-sharing and expert feedback. It was developed from a literature review, grounded in Bandura's self-efficacy theory, and pilot tested with 5 NPs in Phayao Province.
requirements: Participants need computer literacy and internet access; NPs must have at least 1 year of PCU experience per the inclusion criteria
constraints: Evaluated only in Chiang Rai Province over a limited timeframe, which the authors state may limit generalizability
target_learners: Nurse practitioners in primary care units serving agricultural workers exposed to pesticides
target_learning_goals: Occupational health service competency: professional attributes, knowledge, skills, and perceived self-efficacy
examples: The 4-week program integrated 4 self-efficacy strategies: enactive mastery, vicarious experience, verbal persuasion, and emotional arousal.
key_sources: Napamon P, Jirapongsuwan A, Kalampakorn S, Siri S. (2025). The effect of strengthening nurse practitioners’ competency in occupational health services for agricultural workers exposed to pesticides in primary care units, Thailand: a before-and-after study. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2025.22.14

article_title: Effectiveness of a SNAPPS in psychiatric residents assessed using objective structured teaching encounters: a case-control study.
citation: Feijó Lorena Pinho, Pereira Guilherme Abreu, Ruffini Vitor Maia Teles, Valente Fernando Salvetti, dos Santos Renato Antunes, Fakhouri Saadallah Azor Filho, Nunes Maria do Patrocínio Tenório, Augusto Kristopherson Lustosa. (2023). Effectiveness of a SNAPPS in psychiatric residents assessed using objective structured teaching encounters: a case-control study. São Paulo Medical Journal. https://doi.org/10.1590/1516-3180.2021.1028.R1.13072022
title: SNAPPS: a learner-centered case-presentation technique (summarize, narrow, analyze, probe, plan, select)
description: SNAPPS is a six-step technique for clinical case presentation — summarize, narrow, analyze, probe, plan, and select — initially proposed by Wolpaw. The article describes it as based on constructive learning wherein "students as active participants are able to develop new knowledge and teachers are partners in the learning process." It is used here as the intervention taught to residents in a 45-minute lecture within a resident-as-teacher program, and the article reports it can help students verbalize higher-level thinking skills and improve clinical reasoning.
requirements: Delivered as a 45-minute lecture followed by practice, with only the teachers (residents) trained in the technique
constraints: The article notes there have been no previous studies using modified models of SNAPPS for teaching preceptors, and no meta-analysis comparing SNAPPS to traditional training methods
target_learners: psychiatry residents acting as teachers of interns
target_learning_goals: clinical case discussion and teaching of clinical reasoning
examples: Group A residents attended a 45-minute lecture on SNAPPS with videos of simulated cases and instruction on giving effective feedback, then were video-recorded discussing the same three simulated cases
key_sources: Feijó Lorena Pinho, Pereira Guilherme Abreu, Ruffini Vitor Maia Teles, Valente Fernando Salvetti, dos Santos Renato Antunes, Fakhouri Saadallah Azor Filho, Nunes Maria do Patrocínio Tenório, Augusto Kristopherson Lustosa. (2023). Effectiveness of a SNAPPS in psychiatric residents assessed using objective structured teaching encounters: a case-control study. São Paulo Medical Journal. https://doi.org/10.1590/1516-3180.2021.1028.R1.13072022

article_title: Case presentation methods: a randomized controlled trial of the one-minute preceptor versus SNAPPS in a controlled setting.
citation: Fagundes E. D. T., Ibiapina C. C., Alvim C. G., Fernandes R. A. F., Carvalho-Filho M. A., Brand P. L. P. (2020). Case presentation methods: a randomized controlled trial of the one-minute preceptor versus SNAPPS in a controlled setting. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40037-020-00588-y
title: SNAPPS as a learner-centered six-step case-presentation model for expressing clinical reasoning
description: SNAPPS is a mnemonic guiding the learner to structure the case presentation into six steps: Summarize history and findings; Narrow the differential; Analyze the differential; Probe the preceptor about uncertainties; Plan management; and Select case-related issues for self-study. Unlike the OMP method, which gives instructions to teachers, SNAPPS provides them to learners, helping learners understand what is expected of them and take on a central role during the case presentation. The article positions it as both a learning and an assessment tool, allowing teachers to detect gaps in trainees' knowledge or reasoning.
requirements: A 30-minute orientation session demonstrating the technique with an example video and a pocket-sized card listing the six SNAPPS steps sufficed for students to use the method
constraints: Evidence comes from written cases in a controlled setting without the pressure and challenges of real clinical teaching
The rater was not blinded because the methods are clearly different
target_learners: medical students at the beginning of their fifth year
target_learning_goals: expression of clinical reasoning during oral case presentation
examples: Students assigned to the SNAPPS group attended a 30-minute orientation session with a demonstration video and a pocket-sized card listing the six steps
key_sources: Fagundes E. D. T., Ibiapina C. C., Alvim C. G., Fernandes R. A. F., Carvalho-Filho M. A., Brand P. L. P. (2020). Case presentation methods: a randomized controlled trial of the one-minute preceptor versus SNAPPS in a controlled setting. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40037-020-00588-y

article_title: Effectiveness of SNAPPS for improving clinical reasoning in postgraduates: randomized controlled trial.
citation: Jain Vishakha, Rao Siddharth, Jinadani Mariya. (2019). Effectiveness of SNAPPS for improving clinical reasoning in postgraduates: randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education 19: 224. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1670-3
title: SNAPPS: a six-step learner-centered case-presentation model that condenses fact reporting while encouraging clinical reasoning
description: SNAPPS is a six-step mnemonic for case presentations — Summarize history and findings; Narrow differentials; Analyze differentials; Probe preceptor about uncertainties; Plan management; Select case-related issues for self-study. The article describes it as "a learner-centered model, modifies the learning encounter by condensing the reporting of facts while encouraging clinical reasoning," developed from cognitive learning and reflective practice theory and tested here for inpatient postgraduate teaching.
requirements: The article states it "needs brief faculty development for being able to facilitate this technique and an extensive student development for being able to use this technique."
constraints: The article notes "SNAPPS has been used widely for the outpatient or office setting teaching," with inpatient use only cursorily researched before this trial.
target_learners: postgraduate medical residents (MD Medicine) in inpatient ward settings
examples: In the trial, 9 residents used SNAPPS for 3 case presentations each after sensitization sessions, compared with 9 residents giving traditional presentations.
key_sources: Jain Vishakha, Rao Siddharth, Jinadani Mariya. (2019). Effectiveness of SNAPPS for improving clinical reasoning in postgraduates: randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education 19: 224. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1670-3

article_title: Investigating the effects of interprofessional communication education for medical students.
citation: Kim Seung Jae, Kwon Oh Deog, Kim Kyae Hyung, Lee Ji Eun, Lee Seung-Hee, Shin Jwa-Seop, Park Sang Min. (2019). Investigating the effects of interprofessional communication education for medical students. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2019.125
title: 'Communication between healthcare professionals in the clinical field' training session
description: A 3-hour interprofessional communication training for third-year medical students consisting of "small group role-play, small group discussions and presentations, and an overall presentation and discussion for the whole class." 149 students were randomly assigned to 12 small groups of 12–13; each group role-played and video-recorded either a good or a bad example of conflict resolution for one of two conflict cases, evaluated performers with a worksheet, and discussed improvements with a facilitator. The authors position it as the earliest ('isolation') stage of IPE on Harden's spectrum because no other professions participated.
requirements: A facilitator per small group discussion room; cases developed by faculty; video-recording equipment and group discussion rooms
constraints: Not complete IPE because students majoring in other professions did not participate together; groups of 12–13 meant some students only watched role-play; each group addressed only one case and one good-or-bad example
target_learners: Third-year medical students early in clinical rotation
target_learning_goals: Interprofessional communication and conflict resolution skills with other healthcare providers
examples: Groups role-played and filmed a conflict between an intern and a resident or between a resident and a nurse, then discussed positive points or problems with facilitators.
key_sources: Kim Seung Jae, Kwon Oh Deog, Kim Kyae Hyung, Lee Ji Eun, Lee Seung-Hee, Shin Jwa-Seop, Park Sang Min. (2019). Investigating the effects of interprofessional communication education for medical students. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2019.125

article_title: How the study of online collaborative learning can guide teachers and predict students' performance in a medical course.
citation: Saqr Mohammed, Fors Uno, Tedre Matti. (2018). How the study of online collaborative learning can guide teachers and predict students' performance in a medical course. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1126-1
title: Centrality measures taxonomy for educational SNA: quantity of interactions, information relay, and connectedness
description: The article organizes educational social network analysis around centrality measures grouped into three constructs: quantity of interactions (in-degree, out-degree, degree), role in moderating and relaying information (betweenness, information, closeness centrality), and connectedness (eigenvector centrality, eccentricity, clustering coefficient). It notes that "centrality can be calculated in various ways depending on the context" and that each measure captures a distinct aspect of a student's position, from popularity to brokering to social capital. The framework is applied to course-level, thread-level and ego-network analysis of forum interactions.
requirements: Interaction data from an online forum or LMS must be extractable and structured as source-target interactions for network construction.
constraints: The article states interpretation of social networks depends on the context and the design of the course where it occurs.
target_learners: medical undergraduates in blended clinical courses
target_learning_goals: clinical reasoning and case discussion participation
examples: The study calculated in-degree, out-degree, degree, betweenness, information, closeness, eigenvector centrality, eccentricity and clustering for 35 students and linked them to final, clinical and MCQ grades.
key_sources: Saqr Mohammed, Fors Uno, Tedre Matti. (2018). How the study of online collaborative learning can guide teachers and predict students' performance in a medical course. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1126-1
